sweep_summary: German (stan1295) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Féry 1998 (ROA-301, held and verified). The 107 Glottolog title hits are mostly intonation/sentence-prosody/processing papers (about 70 classified prosody-but-not-word-stress, 15 not-relevant or other-variety). Word-stress items proper: Féry 1998, Tomaschek et al. 2023 and Domahs et al. 2008/2014b (already listed); newly fetched sources and read this sweep: Ernestus & Neijt 2008 (MPI PuRe open copy; first-hand CELEX table and pseudoword test - confirms superheavy-final stress and schwa-final penult stress, refines the 'otherwise penult' clause), Domahs et al. 2014a (Frontiers; right-edge three-syllable window, no penult default - confirms), Domahs et al. 2016 (Frontiers; explicit weight summary - confirms), plus Bohn et al. 2011, Wagner & Fischenbeck 2002 and Hirschfeld & Trouvain 2007 (silent on placement). Abstract-only: Röttger et al. 2012 (final-rhyme complexity strongest predictor, probabilistic - confirms; not in our bibliography, high priority), Speyer 2009 (Latinate final-extrametrical reading - refines, medium), Beyermann 2013, Berg 2008, Maczuga 2024. Not obtainable: Domahs/Plag/Carroll 2014b (high), Domahs et al. 2008 (high), Giegerich 1985, Hall 1998 (secondary stress), Ronneberger-Sibold 1998, Lutz 2010, Benware 1987, Jessen et al. 1995, Hale 1969 (not located). Wiese 1996 is on archive.org as a lending copy only. Nothing read contradicts the catalog; no source supersedes Féry 1998.

new_statements.reading: Right-edge, weight-conditioned system: a super-heavy final syllable takes main stress; otherwise the penult is the usual site, with antepenult stress in words whose penult is open/light; schwa syllables never stressed. Their own CELEX count backs this only in part - superheavy finals and schwa finals behave categorically, but words ending in a plain open or closed syllable spread almost evenly over the last three syllables - so the coding stays weight-HEDGED rather than strict QS.

sources.note: Reviews the split between weight-neglecting (Wiese 2000, Levelt 1999) and quantity-sensitive accounts and reports right-to-left assignment works best for simplex words; own NDL model finds word-form n-grams predict stress with high accuracy. fetched sources in the 9/16 audit; confirms the weight-hedged coding.

sources.citation: Domahs, Frank; Blessing, Katharina; Kauschke, Christina; Domahs, Ulrike (2016). Bono Bo and Fla Mingo: Reflections of speech prosody in German second graders' writing to dictation. Frontiers in Psychology 7:856.
sources.quote: Stress assignment is more complicated and largely opaque in words with non-canonical feet or in polysyllabic words. This leads to a general need for lexical specification of stress in German. However, beyond lexicalization there is accumulating evidence for a role of syllable weight in stress assignment, such that light final and closed prefinal syllables are associated with penultimate stress whereas (super) heavy final syllables, especially if combined with light prefinal syllables, lead to stress on the antepenultimate or ultimate syllable (Janßen, 2003; Janßen and Domahs, 2008; Röttger et al., 2012; Domahs et al., 2014).
sources.note: Summary statement by the Marburg group: lexical specification plus a probabilistic weight effect (light final -> penult; superheavy final -> final or antepenult). Matches the catalog's weight-hedged coding; the main study is about children's writing.

sources.citation: Domahs, Frank; Grande, Marion; Huber, Walter; Domahs, Ulrike (2014a). The direction of word stress processing in German: evidence from a working memory paradigm. Frontiers in Psychology 5:574.
sources.quote: Quantity-sensitive accounts state that the structure or weight of the final and/or prefinal syllable is a particularly important predictor of the position of main stress in German (Vennemann, 1991; Féry, 1998; Domahs et al., 2008). Quantity-insensitive accounts typically assume that the PU is the default stress position in German ... Leftward stress computation in German is supported by the fact that only one of the last three syllables (APU, PU, or U) can bear main stress ("three-syllable window," Giegerich, 1985; Vennemann, 1991; Zonneveld et al., 1999).
sources.locator: Introduction p.1 (three-syllable window; QS vs QI accounts) and Discussion p.7
sources.note: Reviews the two positions (weight-sensitive right-edge vs penult-default) and reports non-word reading evidence for leftward (right-edge) computation and against a psychologically real penult default ('we found no evidence for the psychological reality of a default stress position in German', p.6; 'Our data support accounts of German word stress, which assume leftward computation (e.g., Vennemann, 1991; Alber, 1997; Féry, 1998; Domahs et al., 2008)', p.7). Consistent with the catalog's right-edge, weight-hedged coding.

sources.quote: The results of a pseudoword production task suggest that rhyme complexity of the final syllable is a strong predictor of main stress position in German. We also found that antepenult rhyme complexity and orthographic rhyme structure have significant effect on stress assignment. In general, the effects seem to be probabilistic rather than categorical. Our results suggest that phonological theories of German word stress need to allow for multiple probabilistic factors, including syllabic structure of all stressable syllables and orthographic coding.
sources.note: Pseudoword production: final-syllable rhyme complexity (weight) is the strongest predictor, effects probabilistic - the empirical basis for the 'weight-hedged' reading. Not in the per-language bibliography; Cambridge Core PDF link returns the access page.

sources.quote: Word stress in German is usually thought of as following the Germanic stress pattern (main stress on first stem syllable); quasi-monomorphemic words like Forélle or Holúnder suggest, however, that Modern German follows a Latinate stress pattern (last syllable extrametrical; stress on the penultima or the antepenultima, depending on weight of the second-to-last syllable). The change in stress pattern occurred in the 16th and 17th century, judging from evidence of metrical texts, due to a heavy influx of Latin and Romance loan words in this period
sources.note: Abstract-level claim that Modern German quasi-monomorphemic words follow a Latin-type rule (final syllable extrametrical, penult/antepenult by penult weight). Agrees with the catalog on a right-edge weight-conditioned window, but its final-extrametricality contrasts with the catalog's 'heavy final syllable is stressed' clause; full text (De Gruyter, WAF-blocked) needed to see how final-stressed words (Apparat, Manuskript) are handled.
